evening.title: Europe Bets Big On CV90 Armored Fighting Vehicle
evening.text:
Five European NATO members have signed a landmark agreement to jointly procure more than 400 CV90 series infantry fighting vehicles, in a deal valued at approximately $6 billion. The agreement is one of the biggest multinational land systems procurements in recent European history and could offer a model for rebuilding the continent’s armored forces, as NATO seeks to strengthen its posture in the face of the growing threat from Russia.

The contracts were signed today at the Swedish Army Museum in Stockholm, with Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, and the Netherlands participating. The vehicles will be produced by BAE Systems Hägglunds and share a common CV9035 MkIV Nordic Edition configuration, although individual countries will retain differences in terms of equipment, including communications, electronic warfare, and battle management systems.

The significance of the agreement lies not just in the number of vehicles involved. European countries have traditionally procured major land systems through separate national programs, often resulting in different configurations and multiple supply chains, not to mention duplicated development and support costs. The CV90 agreement represents a major effort to overcome those inefficiencies by bringing a group of countries together around a common vehicle configuration, coordinated production, and more closely aligned support arrangements.

In doing so, it provides a tangible example of the kind of multinational defense industrial cooperation European governments have increasingly called for as they seek to rebuild military capabilities following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while at the same time because U.S. security guarantees are now not necessarily taken for granted.

“This joint procurement of the CV90 strengthens NATO’s capabilities and creates opportunities for both effective and close cooperation around the system between our five countries,” Swedish Minister of Defense Pål Jonson said.

There is a long history of European efforts to achieve greater commonality in armored vehicle procurement, and an equally long record of falling short. During the Cold War, attempts to develop a common European tank repeatedly foundered on competing national requirements and disagreements over industrial responsibilities. A Franco-German effort in the late 1950s produced separate national outcomes — the Leopard 1 and AMX-30 — while later Franco-German and Anglo-German projects also failed to deliver a shared tank. Even the ambitious U.S.-German MBT-70 program, intended to replace both countries’ existing tanks with a common design, collapsed amid spiraling costs and incompatible requirements.

NATO did achieve some useful standardization, notably around ammunition and other elements of logistics, but it never translated that into a common fleet of armored vehicles. The result was a collection of national designs, often built around different operational priorities and industrial bases. The CV90 initiative takes a more pragmatic route. Instead of trying to design an entirely new vehicle to satisfy every participant, it brings several countries together around an existing, mature platform and a shared configuration, for a more achievable starting point.

Originally developed in Sweden starting in the mid-1980s, the CV90 already has a substantial NATO footprint. It is in service with Denmark, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, while the Czech Republic and Slovakia have also ordered the type. Switzerland, although not a NATO member, is another established operator, and Ukraine has joined the CV90 user community. BAE Systems lists 10 nations operating or contracted to receive the vehicle, across 17 variants. That gives the Nordic initiative a significant base of existing users with which to share experience, support arrangements, and future upgrades. However, the different national configurations mean that there will be limitations on commonality.

Sweden will acquire 60 CV90 MkIVs under the agreement. Finland is purchasing 160 vehicles in a deal valued at approximately $2.15 billion, including maintenance kits, testing equipment, technical documentation, training, and licenses. Lithuania had previously announced plans to acquire 100 vehicles as part of the multinational program. The remaining quantities for Norway and the Netherlands have not been publicly detailed, although the combined initial order exceeds 400 vehicles.

The Finnish acquisition is particularly significant as Helsinki looks to replace its aging Soviet-era BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles, which are increasingly difficult to support. The new CV90s are expected to begin entering Finnish service from around 2030, while BAE Systems Hägglunds has indicated that deliveries across the broader program could begin as early as 2029.

A Common Platform For A Changing Battlefield

The CV9035 MkIV represents the latest major evolution of the CV90 family, which has developed through successive generations since entering service in the early 1990s. BAE Systems describes it as a fifth-generation iteration of the combat-proven platform, incorporating significant improvements in mobility, payload capacity, electronic architecture, and crew capabilities.

One of the most important changes is the introduction of a Scania diesel engine producing up to 1,000 horsepower, coupled with an upgraded Allison heavy-duty transmission. The drivetrain improvements are intended to provide greater mobility and acceleration while accommodating the additional weight associated with modern protection systems, sensors, and mission equipment.

The MkIV also introduces active damping technology, designed to improve suspension performance, vehicle handling, and stability over difficult terrain. Its gross vehicle weight rating increases from 35 to 37 tonnes, providing a useful boost in payload capacity. This gives operators greater flexibility to accommodate future protection enhancements, sensors, electronic warfare systems, and other mission equipment.

The vehicle also incorporates a NATO-standard electronic architecture and BAE Systems’ iFighting concept, intended to improve crew situational awareness and decision-making through enhanced ergonomics, digital integration, augmented reality, and autonomous support technologies.

Its armament includes a 35mm cannon, co-axial machine gun, and anti-tank guided missiles, providing a combination of direct-fire support and the ability to engage armored targets at longer ranges.

The war in Ukraine has raised serious questions about the survivability and utility of armored vehicles on a modern battlefield in the face of persistent drone threats, in terms of both surveillance and kinetic attack. Nevertheless, the conflict has not rendered armor obsolete. Rather, it has highlighted the challenges of employing armored forces in an increasingly contested battlespace. The continued investment in armored capabilities by major militaries around the world demonstrates that they still regard armored vehicles as an important component of modern land warfare, even as their roles, protection requirements, and methods of employment evolve.

The CV90 has already seen combat use in Ukraine, where Swedish-donated vehicles have been employed by Ukrainian forces. Of the more than 125 CV90s given to Ukraine, at least 25 have been destroyed, damaged, or captured according to the Oryx open-source tracking group. Those figures could be higher, since Oryx only tabulates losses for which it has visual confirmation.

Finland has highlighted the importance of incorporating anti-drone capabilities into its new vehicles. The MkIV’s digital architecture and additional payload capacity will make it easier to integrate future defensive systems, although the precise counter-drone equipment and protection configurations for the five national fleets have not been fully disclosed.

Beyond the military capabilities, the agreement could have a substantial impact on Europe’s ability to manufacture and sustain armored vehicles at scale.

Production will involve companies across the five participating countries, creating a distributed industrial network around BAE Systems Hägglunds’ manufacturing operations in Örnsköldsvik, Sweden. Structural welding for the chassis and turrets will reportedly be concentrated there, while portions of chassis assembly and component production will take place in customer countries.

Major components include the Northrop Grumman Bushmaster III 35mm cannon, a 1,000-horsepower Scania engine, and an Allison transmission.

Finland’s procurement provides one example of the industrial participation involved. Approximately 30 percent of the value of its €1.955 billion contract is expected to remain in Finland, with more than 10 companies involved and Patria playing a major role.

This arrangement should help address the problems that European defense manufacturing has struggled with in terms of fragmented demand and insufficient production capacity. Manufacturers are less likely to make substantial investments in facilities, equipment, and skilled personnel without confidence that orders will extend over several years.

A common procurement involving more than 400 vehicles provides a much more predictable production base than several smaller national orders. It also allows suppliers to plan around larger component requirements, while participating countries gain industrial workshare and greater involvement in maintaining their own fleets.

EDR Online reports that the procurement could generate savings of approximately 10 to 15 percent through bulk purchasing, common components, reduced transportation costs, and standardized production. Shared training, maintenance, and logistics arrangements could produce yet more benefits over the vehicles’ service lives.

A Potential Blueprint For NATO Procurement

The broader implications of the agreement could be considerable. European governments have repeatedly identified the need to reduce fragmentation, increase joint procurement, and strengthen the continent’s defense industrial base. Traditionally, translating those ambitions into actual contracts has proved difficult, particularly when countries have different operational requirements and domestic industrial priorities. Frequently, there are also political considerations to negotiate around.

The CV90 program demonstrates that these obstacles can be overcome, at least among a group of countries with relatively closely aligned requirements.

Potentially, the same principles could be applied to other major land systems, including armored engineering vehicles, recovery platforms, command vehicles, artillery systems, and potentially future main battle tanks.

There are already indications that the CV90 program itself could expand. Finland has an option for an additional 100 vehicles, while subsequent procurement phases could include more of the baseline combat vehicles, specialist variants, and training equipment.

The agreement also strengthens BAE Systems Hägglunds’ position in an increasingly competitive European armored vehicle market. The CV90 family has now surpassed 2,300 vehicles delivered or on order, and the new multinational procurement further reinforces its position as one of Europe’s most established tracked infantry fighting vehicle platforms.

There are important limits to what this agreement demonstrates. It is a major achievement for Northern European defense cooperation, but it does not mean Europe has overcome the fragmentation of its land systems market.

Germany, France, Poland, Italy, and other major European military powers still pursue their own requirements and industrial programs. The continent still operates multiple infantry fighting vehicle families, main battle tank designs, artillery systems, and national support arrangements. Political considerations and domestic industrial interests will continue to complicate attempts to establish common European procurement programs.

Nor does a common vehicle configuration eliminate every interoperability challenge. National communications, electronic warfare, battle management, and other mission systems will continue to differ, while individual armies retain their own operational doctrines and requirements.

Nevertheless, the five-country CV90 agreement offers an example of how multinational procurement can work in practice. It combines a substantial order, a common technical baseline, distributed industrial participation, and the prospect of shared long-term support.

The deal is a major commercial victory for BAE Systems Hägglunds, but it also marks a significant step in European defense cooperation. Five NATO countries are committing to a common armoured vehicle platform on a scale that could make it easier to share spares, support equipment, training, and future upgrades.

The bigger test will be whether other European countries adopt similar arrangements and whether the model can be extended to other systems.

It is a day that lives in infamy forever, and we all know the tale—how the evil Megatron (cursed be the flow of his energon!) commandeered an Autobot shuttle, cruelly murdered its crew, and launched a cowardly surprise attack against Autobot City—a plan utterly bereft of honor, as was so typical of Megatron's schemes. The fearless Autobot transformed, rolled out, and got the job done—even though that cost was high. Many brave Autobots besides Optimus Prime lost their lives during the fighting. It was truly a dark day, a black day—and so, every year on the Friday after Thanksgiving, we pause to remember the noble sacrifices made by Prime and by so many others. evening.title: Indian Company Develops a Helmet Designed to Deflect Incoming Bullets
evening.text:
Pune-based defence firm Technotreon has developed a ballistic helmet which can redirect bullets and so enhance the protection given to military and police personnel.
Indian Patent No. 202011048626 outlines a process which redirects bullets after they make contact with a helmet. Rather than only focusing on a material’s ability to prevent penetration (as is traditionally done), the innovation therefore aims to increase the chance that bullets will instead be redirected from a helmet, and not allow their energy to be passed onto the person wearing it.
Redirect bullets
As stated in the patent, the helmet contains a means of absorbing energy and redirecting bullets. Ideally, bullets should then be diverted away from the head and not simply have their force passed on through the helmet.
Such a helmet may therefore provide extra protection for people facing gunfire from small arms.
Energy absorption is crucial
Apart from preventing penetration, a good quality ballistic helmet also needs to effectively absorb the energy of an impacting bullet.
In addition to absorbing some of a bullet’s energy, Technotreon’s patented invention includes a method of redirecting it. Through this novel process, the interaction between a bullet and helmet is altered to try and lessen the force felt by the wearer.
Unfortunately, the patent does not supply specific information regarding how well the helmet performed, including details of what calibre bullets were fired at it, what level of ballistic protection was achieved and at what speeds the bullets travelled at.
Military uses
There are various areas within both the military and police forces where staff may face ballistic risks and so benefit from this innovation. As well as standard troops, people such as those involved in special forces and on the front line will often require helmets as part of their personal protective gear, particularly in an urban setting.
Whilst there are already various personal protection innovations, a helmet which had both ballistic and energy absorbing properties and could also redirect bullets may prove to be a useful enhancement. Nevertheless, wide scale testing would be essential to determine how well it works and then to ensure that it meets appropriate protection criteria.
Furthering India’s defence innovation
India continues to stimulate defence innovation in the private sector, with firms and start-ups creating a variety of defence related goods including drones, sensors and body and other personal protection.
By producing this new type of helmet, Technotreon is continuing to broaden the scope of home-grown defence innovations being produced by the country’s private sector.

evening.title: Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback
evening.text:
Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028.

That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker, which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers.

The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market.

Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns.

The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC, memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing.

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones.

Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported, memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026.

For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases.

"The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang.

"Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets."

Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years.

Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing.

A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery.

"The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not be interpreted as a return to the old market trajectory," Wang said.

"Some low-end demand has been permanently lost, and the 2028 market will still be about 14 percent below 2025 shipments."

Potential availability of 6G-capable smartphones toward the end of the decade could give the market a boost, but Counterpoint does not expect it to regain its 2025 shipment levels by 2030. ®

evening.title: India and Malaysia conduct joint drills to enhance military interoperability
evening.text:
India and Malaysia are conducting the sixth edition of their joint military exercise, Harimau Shakti, in the Malaysian city of Ipoh, aimed at enhancing military interoperability and further deepening defence ties between the two countries.
In a post on X on Friday, the Indian Army said that personnel from both sides are taking part in a series of joint training activities, including tactical drills and operational planning, to hone their capabilities for sub-conventional operations.
“The 6th edition of the India-Malaysia Joint Military Exercise Harimau Shakti is underway at Ipoh, Malaysia. Troops of both Armies are undertaking joint tactical drills, operational planning and integrated training activities, leveraging modern technologies to refine tactics, techniques and procedures for sub-conventional operations,” the Indian Army posted on X.
“The exercise provides a valuable platform to enhance interoperability, exchange operational experiences and share best practices, while strengthening professional camaraderie, mutual understanding and defence cooperation between India and Malaysia,” it added.
The exercise, which commenced on November 19 and will continue until November 30, involves 120 personnel from each country and focuses on the integrated employment of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and Counter-Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) capabilities, the Ministry of Defence said.
“The aim of the exercise is to jointly rehearse the conduct of sub-conventional operations under Chapter VII of the United Nations mandate, with particular emphasis on synergising responses during counter-terrorism operations. The exercise will focus on coordinated operations in jungle and semi-urban terrain, incorporating joint planning, tactical coordination and the employment of emerging technologies to enhance interoperability and operational effectiveness,” the Defence Ministry said in a statement.
According to the ministry, the exercise was conducted in progressive phases, beginning with cross-training and familiarisation with each other’s operational procedures, followed by joint tactical drills.
“Training activities will include establishment of a Joint Command Post and Surveillance Centre, counter-terrorism operations, raids, cordon-and-search operations and combat engineering drills. Special emphasis will be placed on the integrated employment of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) for reconnaissance and surveillance, along with Counter-Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) capabilities to detect and neutralise hostile drones,” the statement mentioned.
The exercise would culminate in a joint validation exercise involving a simulated counter-terrorism scenario, incorporating coordinated ground operations, integrated surveillance and employment of unmanned systems.

Why Is the Indian Air Force Overhauling MiG-21 Engines After Their Retirement?
evening.text:
The Indian Air Force (IAF) has issued a tender for the reconditioning of 10 Tumansky R-13-300 engines and three diffusers and three power rings. Interest is generated as the R-13-300 is related to previous versions of the MIG 21 plane and not to the now retired MIG-21 Bison which performed its last mission in September 2025.
The tender (2026_IAF_856715_1) was published by Directorate of Engineering (A2) at Air Headquarters (Ref: Air HQ/82103/18/ENG A2 (T2)), on 10th November 2026. There is an earnest money deposit (EMD) of 1.52 crores to be paid to the PCDA Air Force in New Delhi but applicants may apply for a waiver. There is no tender fee.
Applications can be made from 8th December until 21st December (5.30pm). Tender opening will occur on 22nd December (10am). The duration of the contract is 240 days and tenders are valid for 180 days. The procurement uses a two-envelope approach; technical and commercial aspects are dealt with in separate envelopes. For further information, contact should be made with Group Captain Eng A2, Air Headquarters.
Within the procurement scheme, the tender has been allocated to the ‘Civil Works’ category and further specified as for ‘reconditioning of aircraft engines’. It is uncertain whether this reflects the nature of the work to be undertaken or merely serves as a procurement scheme heading. Within the public areas of the procurement site, no contract value has been provided.
R-13-300 and MIG-21 planes
As mentioned above, the R-13-300 engine was employed on previous MIG-21 models such as the Type 96. More recently, the MIG-21bis (after which India based its Bison upgrade programme) was equipped with a more powerful R-25-300 engine.
Consequently, the current tender should not be immediately assumed to be for the MIG-21 Bison which was retired from service last year. On 26th September 2025, the IAF held a formal decommissioning event at Chandigarh. This marked the end of over six decades of MIG-21 service within the Air Force. The Ministry of Defence stated that this was the end of the plane’s active service with the Air Force.
Historically, the IAF has also run a procurement for the reconditioning of R-13, diffusers and power rings for MiG-21 Type-69 planes – again demonstrating how reconditioning of R-13 engines has previously been associated with the older MIG-21 planes. However, this does not clarify what is likely to be the use of the 10 engines detailed in the November 2026 tender.
Why does the IAF require 10 reconditionings?
Whilst the tender does not disclose where the engines are to be deployed or highlight reasons for their reconditioning following the retirement of the MIG-21, various options could exist. Again, however, it is not possible to confirm any of these.
Continuation of pre-retirement servicing and reconditioning arrangements may be one reason. Even post-retirement, repair processes can continue for some time. Particularly where engines and supporting parts have already entered the reconditioning chain, these can take a considerable time to fully process.
Further, the Air Force may be preserving a stock of engines so that they can either continue to be used or be conserved. Alongside the 10 engines, the tender also calls for three diffusers and three power rings to be reconditioned. This implies a bundle of items related to engine reconditioning. Yet, it is not stated whether these are for conservation, disposal or another function.
India has in the past supported allied air forces by providing servicing and supply arrangements. Thus, it is relevant to consider whether the tender relates to export. Nevertheless, there is no indication within the tender that this is the case.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M
evening.text:
Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse.

Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF].

The report, from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million.

The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues.

"The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said.

It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software.

The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems.

Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts. It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor. The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt, an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system.

It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless.

The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay, now rebranded as Civica Income Management.

Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill.

For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools, but that was excluded from the reimplementation.

Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example.

A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026.

Council taxpayers can be assured the new system has gone live without major problems, but that is hardly cause for celebration. ®

Its counsel, Harish Salve, told the court that the board needed to meet to comply with a Reserve Bank of India directive requiring the company to inform the central bank by December 12 of its decision on the mandated listing.Representing the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, Abhishek Manu Singhvi argued that the RBI deadline was being used to create artificial urgency around the meeting.(With inputs from PTI)

evening.title: UK government rejects national consultation on AI datacenters
evening.text:
The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures.

Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed.

The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared.

In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027.

"Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says.

"Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI."

But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests.

This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance.

The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning.

Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources.

If this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows.

The Covenant sets out efficiency targets and reporting expectations, but does not explain how compliance will be enforced or specify penalties for failing to meet its tests.

Protect the Wild notes that it "barely acknowledges wildlife, habitats or biodiversity. In fact, it doesn't mention any of those things at all."

The Covenant does, however, call on operators to "protect nature," without spelling out specific safeguards for wildlife, habitats, or biodiversity.

While the government encourages all server farms to meet the tests, only those it considers "strategic" are required to do so, as we noted above. And even that is only in order to qualify for extra government support, not in order to gain approval for a project.

Further, the campaign group contends that having environmental concerns addressed on a project-by-project basis at the planning level is a major barrier to tackling greenhouse gas emissions at a national level.

It cites the draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, under which operational emissions from nationally significant projects in England, including those from on-site power generation, would be managed against national climate commitments at an economy-wide level rather than assessing each application's contribution to those targets.

Protect the Wild also argues that project-level assessments do not adequately capture nationwide habitat loss, even though the planning process requires consideration of cumulative environmental effects.

Datacenters have become a growing public concern in the UK, although opposition has not reached the level it has in the US, where anti-datacenter sentiment played a major part in political campaigns for the recent midterm elections.

But there were protests around the country at the start of November, such as in London and at Great Torrington, a town in Devon where a proposed 1.5 GW data campus and battery energy storage facility would cover 850 acres of nearby farmland.

Celebrity TV cook Delia Smith recently joined protests over a proposed datacenter on the edge of Norwich in Norfolk over concerns it may threaten a nearby nature reserve.

Protesters are unlikely to find much sympathy in Westminster. The government has already pinned its hopes for growing the economy on AI, as detailed in its AI Opportunities Action Plan last year, and it sees building more datacenters as key to achieving this.

The Guardian reports that Natural England, the government's own advisory body for the natural environment, is being threatened with abolition weeks after raising objections to a large AI campus near Bristol because of the threat it poses to protected wildlife and habitats.

A separate report found that the government met with 137 different businesses to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, but did not meet a single community group or environmental organization during the same period. ®

evening.title: Europe's AI sovereignty push: Lots of cloud, not much silver lining
evening.text:
Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles.

Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China.

"The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register.

He said Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where new technologies replace old ones.

Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent.

Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment.

"For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use."

The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced new rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much.

"Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign.

"They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us.

Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach.

"The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®

AI boom leaves network operators waiting up to 18 months for kit
evening.text:
The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN.

RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.

As Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN says optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months.

This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders. The issue now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies.

In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening.

The sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN says. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the issue.

However, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time.

Network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now.

The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly.

RETN also says AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available.

Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year.

For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site.

Some developers are prepared to swallow the cost: RETN says a major cloud provider is exploring converting an abandoned factory in Central Europe into a large-scale server farm, despite little existing fiber in the area.

However, RETN's warning is that connectivity must be planned alongside power and construction, not left until the datacenter is nearly ready to open. ®

evening.title: Royal Navy orders £142M in minehunting drones from US supplier
evening.text:
Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).

These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a "Hybrid Navy" comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges.

The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620, built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company.

We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry.

The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII says it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting.

HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations.

The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open.

By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class, but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems.

The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP, an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance.

The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD.

"This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP.

Like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy.

In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®

evening.title: Support team put in an emergency order for vodka – lots of vodka – to bring PCs back online
evening.text:
The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.

"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.

The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.

"We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore."

Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.

Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.

One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.

And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.

When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded.

Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.

"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register.

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol."

As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.

"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.

By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.

"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.

The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

"It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

Have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®

evening.title: AWS adds virtual iPhones to its cloud
evening.text:
AWS now offers two new types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

The cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS.

AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices.

“With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement.

AWS also says developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues.

That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland.

When The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu.

At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0.

Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10th place.

iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list.

Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors.

evening.title: Free e-government platform that serves two billion people in ten countries has critical SQL injection bug
evening.text:
India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.

The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants.

DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities.

India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka

India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.”

“An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.”

eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem.

While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities.

Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®
